name: Phenobarbital
route_note: Oral tablets and elixir; IV or IM injection for status epilepticus and neonatal seizures.

discovery.note: Synthesised at Bayer in 1911 as a hypnotic; the young psychiatrist Hauptmann noticed that it suppressed seizures in his epilepsy patients.

tagline: The oldest anticonvulsant still in wide use, and a WHO essential medicine
summary: Phenobarbital, introduced by Bayer in 1912, is the oldest antiseizure medicine still widely used. It is inexpensive and effective, making it a first-line option in low-resource settings and for neonatal seizures, though sedation and enzyme induction limit its use elsewhere.
mechanism: Phenobarbital binds GABA-A receptors at a site distinct from benzodiazepines and prolongs the opening of their chloride channels, enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission; at high concentrations it opens the channel directly.
It also reduces glutamate-mediated excitation through AMPA/kainate receptors and blocks some calcium channels. It is a potent inducer of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes.

history.title: Barbital
history.detail: Emil Fischer and Joseph von Mering introduce barbital, the first barbiturate hypnotic.

history.title: Synthesis
history.detail: Heinrich Hörlein at Bayer synthesises phenobarbital.

history.title: Luminal and epilepsy
history.detail: Bayer launches Luminal as a sedative; Alfred Hauptmann reports its anticonvulsant effect.

history.title: International control
history.detail: Phenobarbital is placed under Schedule IV of the UN Convention on Psychotropic Substances.

history.title: First FDA approval
history.detail: Sezaby (phenobarbital sodium powder for injection) becomes the first FDA-approved phenobarbital, for neonatal seizures; earlier US products were marketed without approval.

pk.half_life: about 80 hours on average (53–118 h) in adults
pk.metabolism: hepatic (CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2E1) and N-glucosidation; strong enzyme inducer
pk.excretion: renal, about 25% unchanged; enhanced by urine alkalinisation

common: Cognitive and behavioural effects (especially in children)
serious: Respiratory depression (especially with other CNS depressants)

facts: Phenobarbital has been on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines since the first list in 1977.
Its very long half-life allows once-daily dosing, which is useful where access to medicines is irregular.
